title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
short: Gunpowder formulas appear in China by 1044 and in Arabic and Latin texts by the later 1200s, but the path between them is unattested.
matters: The route determines whether gunpowder should be described as a Mongol-era transfer across Eurasia, a product of Mamluk and Andalusian Arabic chemistry, or a partly independent European development from Chinese-derived saltpetre knowledge. It shapes debates over the 'military revolution', over the role of the Mongol empire as a conduit of technology, and over the place of the Islamic world in histories of chemistry and warfare that often move directly from China to Europe.
stuck: The Chinese Wujing zongyao (compiled c. 1040–1044) gives the earliest surviving formulas, but the next datable recipes appear almost simultaneously in the 1260s–1290s in Latin (Roger Bacon's allusions in the Opus maius and Opus tertium, c. 1267; the Liber ignium attributed to Marcus Graecus) and in Arabic (Ḥasan al-Rammāḥ, c. 1270s–1280s), with no text recording a transfer. Arabic terms such as naft and Latin descriptions of incendiaries are ambiguous about whether they mean gunpowder, and the dating of many recipe collections rests on late manuscript copies. Bacon's supposed anagram recipe has been regarded as doubtful since the early twentieth century.
solved: A securely dated text, or a stemma of dated manuscripts, that shows one of the Latin or Arabic gunpowder recipe traditions copying or translating from an identifiable earlier source in another language, so that the direction and approximate date of transfer can be stated. A dated Persian, Arabic or Latin witness of a saltpetre-based recipe earlier than the 1260s outside China would also count.
approach: Agents can assemble a comparative corpus of every dated gunpowder and saltpetre recipe in Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Latin, normalising ingredient proportions, technical vocabulary and purification methods, and then test for textual dependence between traditions. This requires digitizing and transcribing Arabic and Persian furūsiyya and military manuscripts in Paris, Istanbul, Cairo and elsewhere, and the earliest Latin Liber ignium and Feuerwerkbuch witnesses, with codicologists dating the copies.

existing.title: Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom: A Challenge to a Mediaeval Society
existing.note: Dated securely attested Mamluk firearms to the 1360s and cautioned against reading earlier naft references as gunpowder.

existing.title: A History of Greek Fire and Gunpowder
existing.venue: Cambridge: Heffer (repr. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1999)
existing.note: Foundational survey of Chinese, Arabic and Latin incendiary and gunpowder texts; dated the Liber ignium gunpowder recipes to about 1300 and argued for Chinese priority.

existing.authors: Joseph Needham, with Ho Ping-Yü, Lu Gwei-Djen and Wang Ling
existing.title: Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5, pt. 7: Military Technology; The Gunpowder Epic
existing.note: Comprehensive treatment of Chinese gunpowder from the Wujing zongyao onward, proposing transmission to Europe via the Mongols.

existing.authors: Lu Gwei-Djen, Joseph Needham and Phan Chi-Hsing
existing.title: The Oldest Representation of a Bombard
existing.note: Argued that a Sichuan cave sculpture shows a gun by about 1128, pushing Chinese firearms well before the European record.

existing.title: Weapons and Warfare in Renaissance Europe: Gunpowder, Technology, and Tactics
existing.note: Discussed saltpetre supply and the European recipe tradition and was sceptical of attributing a single route to transmission.

existing.title: Gunpowder Composition for Rockets and Cannon in Arabic Military Treaties of the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Centuries
existing.note: Argued from al-Rammāḥ and other Arabic treatises for an Arabic-Islamic intermediary stage, including early Mamluk and Andalusian cannon; several of its dating claims are disputed.

existing.title: Firearms: A Global History to 1700
existing.note: Comparative global history that accepts Chinese origin and treats the transmission route as uncertain.

existing.title: Gunpowder and Firearms: Warfare in Medieval India
existing.note: Traced gunpowder into South Asia with the Mongols in the thirteenth century, supporting a Mongol-era diffusion model.

existing.title: The Mongol Empire – the First 'Gunpowder Empire'?
existing.venue: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society 23 (3): 441–469
existing.note: Assessed the evidence for Mongol use and diffusion of gunpowder weapons and argued that it was more limited than often claimed.

existing.title: The Gunpowder Age: China, Military Innovation, and the Rise of the West in World History
existing.note: Global synthesis that places the arrival of gunpowder in Europe in the context of Mongol-era contact.

existing.title: Gunpowder Technology in the Fifteenth Century: A Study, Edition and Translation of the Firework Book
existing.venue: Woodbridge: Boydell Press (Royal Armouries Research Series 3)
existing.note: First full edition and translation of a Feuerwerkbuch manuscript (Royal Armouries I.34), clarifying the later European recipe tradition against which earlier sources must be read.

archives.collection: Département des Manuscrits: Arabic military (furūsiyya) treatises, including copies of al-Rammāḥ, and Latin manuscripts of the Liber ignium
archives.note: Holds manuscripts used by nineteenth-century editors of both the Arabic and Latin traditions; many are on Gallica, others only described in the catalogue.

archives.collection: Latin and German manuscripts of the Liber ignium, Feuerwerkbuch and fifteenth-century Kriegsbücher
archives.note: Large holdings of German pyrotechnic and military manuscripts, many digitized through the Münchener Digitalisierungszentrum.

archives.collection: Library manuscript RA I.34 (Firework Book) and related military manuscripts
archives.note: Witness edited by Müller (2024); access by appointment.

archives.collection: Ming-period editions and manuscript copies of the Wujing zongyao
archives.note: The Song printings are lost, so all surviving witnesses of the 1044 formulas are later reprints whose textual history needs collation.

archives.collection: Wujing zongyao (digitized transcription and page images)
archives.note: Searchable online text of the Wujing zongyao, useful for terminological comparison; requires checking against printed editions.
